documents.title: Mission and Theory of Change
documents.content:
# Bright Orbit STEM Lab — Mission and Theory of Change

Bright Orbit STEM Lab, Inc. is a 501(c)(3) public charity incorporated in Michigan in 2015 and based in Detroit, Michigan. Programmes run in Wayne County, Michigan.

## Mission
Bright Orbit STEM Lab helps girls in grades 6-12 in Detroit build the skills, confidence and connections to pursue careers in science, technology, engineering and math.

## Why it matters
In our 2025 intake survey, 62% of incoming club members said they did not know any woman who works in technology or engineering. 84% of the girls we serve qualify for free or reduced-price lunch, so an unpaid internship is not an option for most of them.

## Theory of change
If girls from low-income Detroit families get hands-on robotics and coding practice with other girls, see women working in technology, and earn a paid first job in the field, then they will see themselves in STEM careers and take the next step into college or STEM training. Confidence and real work experience in high school are what turn interest into a career path.

documents.title: Programme Descriptions
documents.content:
# Programme Descriptions

## Orbit Clubs
After-school robotics and coding clubs that meet twice a week for two hours at 14 partner schools in Detroit (9 middle schools and 5 high schools). Paid coaches lead each club; girls build competition robots and learn Python and web design. 640 girls took part in 2025-26.

## Launchpad Summer Engineering Camp
A free four-week, full-day camp (weekdays, 9am to 3pm) each July at our Midtown Detroit lab. Campers design, build and test engineering prototypes in small teams. Meals and bus passes are provided. 180 girls attended in summer 2025.

## Senior Tech Internships
Paid 10-week spring internships for high-school seniors with 22 local employers in Detroit and Dearborn. Interns work 125 hours at $16 an hour ($2,000 each) and are paired with a volunteer mentor. 48 seniors completed internships in 2025-26.

## Plans
- Add 4 Orbit Clubs in 2027-28 (about 180 more girls).
- Grow internships to 60 seniors once new host employers are confirmed.

documents.title: 2025-26 Impact Report
documents.content:
# 2025-26 Impact Report

## Who we serve
- 820 unique girls across our three programmes (some take part in more than one).
- 640 girls in Orbit Clubs, 180 campers at Launchpad, 48 senior interns.
- 79% are Black, 12% Hispanic/Latina, 5% Middle Eastern or North African, 4% white or multiracial.
- 84% qualify for free or reduced-price lunch; 61% are in grades 6-8 and 39% in grades 9-12.

## Outcomes
- The share of club members who said they can see themselves in a STEM career rose from 38% in the fall to 71% in the spring.
- 26 club robotics teams competed in regional competitions; 9 advanced to the state championship.
- 166 of 180 campers (92%) completed all four weeks of Launchpad.
- Of 48 interns, 45 (94%) graduated from high school and 39 (81%) enrolled in college or a STEM training programme by fall 2026. 11 interns were offered part-time jobs by their host employers.

## In their words
"Before Orbit Club I thought coding was for boys. Now I'm teaching my little brother Python." — ninth-grade club member

## How we measure
Pre/post surveys each fall and spring, plus a shared attendance database.

documents.title: FY2026 Budget Summary
documents.content:
# FY2026 Budget Summary

Annual operating budget (FY2026, July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026): $1.9 million.

## Expenses
- Programme staff (club coaches, camp instructors, internship coordinator): $860,000
- Robotics kits, laptops and materials: $175,000
- Intern wages (48 interns at $2,000 each): $96,000
- Launchpad camp meals, bus passes and field trips: $124,000
- Robotics competitions and Spring Showcase Night: $65,000
- Administration and finance: $330,000
- Fundraising: $250,000
- Total: $1,900,000

## Revenue mix
- Foundations: 48%
- Corporate gifts and employer partners: 24%
- Individual donors: 15%
- Government (City of Detroit youth services contract): 8%
- Events: 5%

Cost per girl served: about $2,300 per year (820 girls).

documents.title: Governance and Capacity
documents.content:
# Governance and Capacity

- Board of 13 directors; meets quarterly. The board includes three engineers from local employers and a former Detroit high school principal.
- Most recent audit: FY2025 independent audit completed, clean opinion.
- Staff: 16 full-time, 9 part-time, and about 110 volunteer mentors, most of them women working in technology and engineering.
- Key leaders: Nia Hollins, Executive Director (founded Bright Orbit in 2015 after 12 years as a software engineer); Priya Raman, Director of Development; Danielle Okafor, Grants Manager.
- One full-time grants manager; the director of development spends about 40% of her time on grants.
- No experience yet managing a federal grant directly.
- Policies in place: child safeguarding policy, background checks for all staff and mentors, conflict of interest policy, whistleblower policy, and a signed workplace safety agreement with every internship host employer.
- Programme data (attendance, surveys, intern follow-up) is kept in a shared database and reported to the board each quarter.

# Organisation Overview (approved language)

Bright Orbit STEM Lab helps girls in grades 6-12 in Detroit build the skills, confidence and connections to pursue careers in science, technology, engineering and math. Since 2015 we have run after-school robotics and coding clubs at partner schools, a free summer engineering camp, and paid internships that give high-school seniors their first job in technology with a local employer. In 2025-26 we served 820 girls. Over the year, the share of club members who said they can see themselves in a STEM career rose from 38% to 71%, and 81% of our senior interns enrolled in college or STEM training.

Lakeshore Workforce Futures Fund — Next-Generation Talent Grants (FICTIONAL SAMPLE)
The Fund invests in Michigan nonprofits that connect young people aged 12-18 to the skills and employers behind the state's technology, engineering and skilled-trades jobs. Priority goes to programmes that reach girls and young people of colour from low-income households, and to programmes with paid work-based learning. Awards range from $50,000 to $100,000 for one year. No match is required. Applicants must be Michigan-based 501(c)(3) organisations with at least two years of outcome data. Funds may not be used for capital or building costs or for scholarships paid to individuals. Applications are due by 5pm Eastern on the deadline date and must include four narrative responses, an organisational and programme budget, the most recent audit or financial review, and a list of employer partners. Grantees submit an interim report at six months and a final outcomes report at 12 months.

questions.answer: Bright Orbit is the leading provider of STEM education for girls in Michigan. We serve over 1,000 girls every year across the state with amazing programmes that truly change lives. Our internships place nearly all of our seniors into great jobs, and basically all of them go on to college. We are passionate about making a difference and we believe girls can do anything. With your support, we will keep doing what we do best and reach even more girls.

questions.prompt: Describe the programme you are requesting funding for and who it serves.
questions.answer: We are requesting support for Orbit Clubs, our after-school robotics and coding clubs for girls in grades 6-12. Clubs meet twice a week for two hours at 14 partner schools in Detroit: 9 middle schools and 5 high schools. Paid coaches lead each club, and girls build competition robots and learn Python and web design. In 2025-26, 640 girls took part. The girls we serve reflect the neighbourhoods we work in: 79% are Black, 12% are Hispanic/Latina and 5% are Middle Eastern or North African, and 84% qualify for free or reduced-price lunch. questions.prompt: What outcomes do you expect, and how will you measure them?
questions.answer: We focus on two outcomes for club members. The first is STEM career identity: in 2025-26, the share of club members who said they can see themselves in a STEM career rose from 38% in the fall to 71% in the spring. We measure progress with pre/post surveys of STEM confidence and career identity each fall and spring, and we track attendance in a shared database. Programme data is reported to our board of 13 directors each quarter, so we can spot clubs that need extra support early in the year.

questions.prompt: Describe the need your project addresses.
questions.answer: Girls in Detroit rarely see a path into technology and engineering careers. In our 2025 intake survey, 62% of incoming club members said they did not know any woman who works in technology or engineering. Money is a second barrier: 84% of the girls we serve qualify for free or reduced-price lunch, so an unpaid internship is not an option for most of them. Senior Tech Internships close both gaps. Seniors earn $16 an hour for 125 hours over a 10-week spring internship with a local employer, and each intern is paired with a volunteer mentor. In 2025-26, 48 seniors completed internships with 22 employers in Detroit and Dearborn, and 11 were offered part-time jobs by their host employers.

questions.prompt: Describe your organisation's track record with this population.
questions.answer: Since 2015, Bright Orbit STEM Lab has worked with girls in grades 6-12 in Detroit. In 2025-26 we served 820 girls across three programmes: Orbit Clubs at 14 partner schools, the Launchpad Summer Engineering Camp and Senior Tech Internships. Of the 48 seniors who completed paid internships, 45 (94%) graduated from high school and 39 (81%) enrolled in college or a STEM training programme by fall 2026. Across our clubs, the share of girls who said they can see themselves in a STEM career rose from 38% in the fall to 71% in the spring. library_answers.question: Why is your organisation well positioned to do this work?
library_answers.answer: Bright Orbit STEM Lab has worked with girls in grades 6-12 in Detroit since 2015, and our founder, Nia Hollins, spent 12 years as a software engineer before starting it. In 2025-26 we served 820 girls across Orbit Clubs at 14 partner schools, the Launchpad Summer Engineering Camp and Senior Tech Internships with 22 local employers. Our results show the model works: the share of club members who can see themselves in a STEM career rose from 38% to 71% over the year, and of our 48 senior interns, 94% graduated from high school and 81% enrolled in college or a STEM training programme. About 110 volunteer mentors, most of them women working in technology and engineering, give girls role models they rarely meet otherwise. We are well run, too: our FY2025 independent audit received a clean opinion, a board of 13 meets quarterly, and a full-time grants manager oversees every funder report.

program_report.title: Programme Progress Report: September 1 – October 31, 2026
program_report.content:
# Programme Progress Report: September 1 – October 31, 2026

## Grant
Belle Isle Engineering Trust — Robotics in Every Classroom Fund, $60,000 for Orbit Clubs (September 1, 2026 – August 31, 2027).

## Delivered so far
All 14 Orbit Clubs (9 middle schools and 5 high schools) opened in the week of September 8. Each club meets twice a week for two hours with a paid coach. By October 31 we had held 224 club sessions (16 per club). Girls began building their first competition robots and started Python lessons.

## Participants
- 598 girls enrolled in Orbit Clubs so far this school year.
- 80% Black, 11% Hispanic/Latina, 5% Middle Eastern or North African, 4% white or multiracial.
- 85% qualify for free or reduced-price lunch.

## Early results
- Average attendance: 83% of enrolled girls at each session.
- Fall baseline survey: 37% said they can see themselves in a STEM career (38% last fall; spring 2026 result was 71%).
- 26 robotics teams registered for the winter regional competitions.

## In their words
"I wired my first motor this week and it actually moved." — sixth-grade club member

## Spending to date
$21,400 of $60,000 (36%): $12,600 in coach stipends and $8,800 for 22 robotics kits and materials.

## Next steps
Regional competitions in January–February and the spring post-survey in May.

program_report.title: Programme Progress Report: July 1 – October 31, 2026
program_report.content:
# Programme Progress Report: July 1 – October 31, 2026

## Grant
Great Lakes Girls' Futures Foundation — Summer STEM Access Grants, $75,000 for Launchpad Summer Engineering Camp (July 1, 2026 – June 30, 2027).

## Delivered so far
Launchpad ran for four weeks in July 2026, weekdays from 9am to 3pm at our Midtown Detroit lab. Campers worked in small teams to design, build and test engineering prototypes, including water filters, wind-powered cars and a robotic arm. The camp ended with a family showcase on the final Friday.

## Participants
- 178 girls enrolled; 165 (93%) completed all four weeks.
- 86% qualify for free or reduced-price lunch.
- 72% were rising 7th and 8th graders.

## Removing barriers
- 6,920 breakfasts and lunches served.
- 164 monthly bus passes issued; 12 campers were driven by family members.

## Early results
On the end-of-camp survey, 74% of campers said they can see themselves in a STEM career, up from 41% on the first day. 58 campers have since joined an Orbit Club this fall.

## In their words
"My team's car went the farthest. I want to be an engineer now." — seventh-grade camper

## Spending to date
$52,300 of $75,000 (70%): $31,500 for camp meals, $14,800 for bus passes and field trips, and $6,000 toward camp instructors.

## Next steps
Recruitment for summer 2027 begins in March; the remaining funds cover planning and instructor hiring.
